div.head: Geþyncðo 6
div.ab: ⁊ gif mássere geþeah, þæt he ferde þrige ofer wíd sǽ be his agenum cræfte, se wæs þonne syððan þegenrihtes weorðe.
Et si massere ascenderet, ut ter magnum mare transfretaret per proprium negotium suum, fuit deinde taini dignus rectitudine.
[62] Si mercator ter mare transisset suo proprio sumptu, talis deinde erat liberalitate dignus, quod dicunt þegenrihtes þurðe.
And gif massere geþeah þæt he ferde þrige ofer widsæ be his agenum cræfte, se wæs þonne syððan þegenrihtes weorðe.
Und wenn ein Kaufmann [so] emporkam, dass er dreimal vermöge seiner eigenen Geschäftskraft übers offene Meer fuhr, der genoss dann fortan Thegnberechtigung.
And if a merchant prospered [so] that he crossed the open sea three times by his own means, he was thereafter entitled to thegn-right.
And if a trader prospered, that he crossed thrice the open sea at his own expense, he was then afterwards entitled to the rights of a thegn.]
And if a merchant prospered so that he fared three times over the open sea by his own means, he was afterward worthy of a thane’s rights.

Nicht ‘Schiff’, wie Bo.-Toller und Frühere meinten; vgl.: his agnes cræftes ‘of his own strength’ Bo.-Toller. Die für ‘Schiff’ zitierte Stelle in Cynewulfs Andreas 500 erklären als ‘Kunst’ Grein und Symonds Cynewulfs Wortschatz. Murray New Engl. dict. belegt craft: ‘vessel’ erst seit 17. Jh.

Not ‘ship’, as Bo.-Toller and earlier scholars thought; cf.: his agnes cræftes ‘of his own strength’ Bo.-Toller. The passage cited for ‘ship’ in Cynewulf’s Andreas 500 is explained as ‘skill’ by Grein and Symonds Cynewulfs Wortschatz. Murray New Engl. dict. attests craft: ‘vessel’ only from the 17th cent.

Bessere im Text widsæ: Ein Wort. Gemeint ist vielleicht nur die Fahrt von England nach Frankreich, Deutschland oder Skandinavien (nicht notwendig der offene Ozean), im Ggs. zur Fahrt auf Binnengewässern und längs Britischer Küste, jedenfalls nicht das Mittelmeer (gegen Schanz Engl. Handelspol. I 133. 355)

In the text read widsæ as one word. What is meant is perhaps only the voyage from England to France, Germany or Scandinavia (not necessarily the open ocean), in contrast to voyages on inland waters and along the British coast; at any rate not the Mediterranean (against Schanz Engl. Handelspol. I 133. 355)

Vgl. Gl Handel 14—c und 17 über Æthelreds II. Handelsverträge. Nordischen Einfluss sehen in dieser Begünstigung des Seehändlers im Ggs. zur niederen Stellung Agsächs. Kleinhandels auch Cunningham Growth § 40, Steenstrup Danelag 105, A. Bugge in Reallex. Germ. Altt. 429

Cf. Gl Handel 14—c and 17 on Æthelred II’s commercial treaties. Norse influence is seen in this favouring of the sea-trader, in contrast to the low position of Anglo-Saxon petty trade, also by Cunningham Growth § 40, Steenstrup Danelag 105, A. Bugge in Reallex. Germ. Altt. 429
